title: No balm in Gilead? (Jeremiah 8:18–22)
hookLine: the weeping prophet asks why his people aren't healed; later a spiritual answered, there is a balm

lines: SOME PLACES ARE KNOWN FOR ONE THING.
cards: Some places are known for one thing. Champagne, Florida oranges, Swiss watches. In the Bible, it's balm from Gilead, the hill country east of the Jordan River.
It was a fragrant resin, prized as medicine for wounds. In Genesis, the caravan that buys young Joseph from his brothers is coming from Gilead, camels loaded with balm, bound for Egypt.
In the Bible's world, Gilead meant medicine. So when the prophet Jeremiah wanted to say how bad things had become, he asked a question that would sound almost absurd.

teach.h: THE MEDICINE EXISTS. WHY NO HEALING?
teach.b: In the King James Bible: "Is there no balm in Gilead; is there no physician there? why then is not the health of the daughter of my people recovered?"
The medicine exists, the doctors exist, so why are my people still sick? Jeremiah has been nicknamed the weeping prophet, and this passage shows why.
Just before it, he grieves: "The harvest is past, the summer is ended, and we are not saved." The season for rescue has come and gone.
Just after, he wishes his head were waters and his eyes a fountain of tears, to weep day and night.

Earlier in the chapter, he complains that other prophets were treating the people's wound lightly, saying "Peace, peace; when there is no peace." Jeremiah won't paper over the wound. He'd rather weep.
And in these verses it's hard to tell who's speaking. Jeremiah, or God?
The voices blur, as if God's grief and the prophet's are the same tears.
Long after, an African American spiritual turned Jeremiah's question into an answer.

teach.h: IS THERE NO BALM IN GILEAD?
teach.b: The song begins: there is a balm in Gilead. Not is there. There is.

In the song, the balm points to Jesus, the healer. People singing out of hard lives answered yes. The honest question and the answer belong together: tears that don't pretend, and hope that doesn't give up.

how: Christians sing the African American spiritual "There Is a Balm in Gilead," and some churches read Jeremiah 8 in services of lament and in prayers for the sick.

o: Jeremiah's nickname, for grieving his people's wound
Jeremiah's name for the prophets who cried peace, peace
a title for any prophet who spoke at funerals

games.q: what's inside Jeremiah 8 — tap the pairs.
p: hill country east of the Jordan
turned the question into an answer

s: Gilead's balm appears in the Joseph story
the caravan that buys Joseph is coming from Gilead with balm.
Jeremiah says there is a balm in Gilead
he asks, is there no balm? the spiritual later turned the question into an answer.
in these verses, it's always clear who's speaking
the voices of Jeremiah and God seem to blur, as if they share the grief.

games.q: you're Jeremiah. your people are deeply wounded, and other prophets are saying peace, peace. what do you do?
o: join them and say all is well.
blame the people and walk away.
games.why: he won't treat the wound lightly. he asks why the people aren't healed, and wishes his eyes were a fountain of tears.

practice: Bring to mind someone who is hurting, someone sick or grieving, someone whose wound others treat lightly, and don't rush to fix it in your head; let Jeremiah's question stand for a moment.
Then picture a balm laid gently on that wound: rest, care, a doctor's skill, a friend's presence.
If you pray, pray for their healing in your own words; if not, hold them in your attention with care, and think of one way to bring a little balm.

wordCard.voice: Weeping prophet. Jeremiah's nickname, earned by grief like this: asking why his people stay wounded when the medicine already exists.

orig.note: Hebrew: balm, a healing resin. the medicine Gilead was well-known for.

carryVoice: Your line: there is a balm. Not a fix, but something soothing laid on a wound. Go gently.
